analysis.one_liner: Replaces private military contractors with government personnel for security and war-zone critical functions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee in February 2010 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2011, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the State Department to use only government employees—not hired security companies—to guard U.S. embassies and consulates in Iraq and Afghanistan, and set a deadline of January 1, 2011 for moving mission-critical war work (security, training, interrogation, intelligence, prison administration) from contractors back to government and military personnel. It also would have forced defense and diplomatic agencies to hand Congress copies of every Iraq and Afghanistan contract over $5 million and report the number of contractors killed or wounded and any discipline taken against them.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund these contracts and would get real accounting for them; U.S. soldiers, whose mission the bill argued was undermined by contractors; civilians in war zones, since contractor misconduct (the Nisour Square shooting killed 17 Iraqis) would face stricter checks; and Congress, which the bill found lacked even basic information about how many contractors were deployed, how many died, or what discipline they faced.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and U.S. troops in war zones

how_it_helps.text: Required the State Department to ensure all security at U.S. diplomatic missions in Iraq and Afghanistan is provided by U.S. government personnel, not contractors, within 180 days of enactment [S3].

Required a presidential plan to transition mission-critical and emergency-essential functions—protective services, training, weapons repair, prison administration, interrogation, intelligence—away from private contractors by January 1, 2011, with certifications of background checks, criminal jurisdiction over contractors, and whistleblower protections if the deadline slipped [S2][S3].

Gave specified congressional committees access to copies of every Iraq and Afghanistan contract over $5 million from DoD, State, Interior, and USAID dating back to October 2001, and required reports on contractor headcounts, total cost, deaths and injuries, and disciplinary actions [S2][S3].
Allowed contract renewals only if the agency certified it lacked government personnel and contractors passed background checks and were subject to U.S. criminal jurisdiction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private military and security contractors—companies like Blackwater/Xe, DynCorp, and ArmorGroup—would lose lucrative war-zone contracts, and defense and diplomatic agencies would bear the cost of hiring and training government employees to replace them. An honest supporter would also acknowledge that hiring and training enough government personnel for these functions is expensive and slow, which is why the bill required agencies to explain any missed deadlines.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private military contractors and their federal contracts

drawbacks.text: Transitioning security, training, and intelligence work to government personnel requires recruiting, training, and paying a much larger federal workforce, and the bill itself anticipated agencies might miss the January 1, 2011 deadline by requiring them to explain why and submit a plan [S3].

Contractors can be hired and released flexibly as missions surge and shrink; a permanent government workforce for fluctuating war-zone needs is costlier to maintain between conflicts, an objection the bill's renewal-exception process implicitly acknowledged [S3].

The bill's findings section catalogs contractor abuses, including the 2007 Nisour Square shooting in which Blackwater contractors killed 17 Iraqis and a judge later dismissed criminal charges over prosecutorial evidence problems—illustrating the accountability gap the bill targeted but also the difficulty of prosecuting war-zone misconduct regardless of employer [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits—ending armed contractor misconduct like the Nisour Square shooting, closing the tax and billing abuses documented in the findings, and giving Congress actual sight of who works and dies under these contracts—address problems the bill documents in detail with government audit findings [S3]. The costs are real but conventional: replacing contractors with government employees costs money and lead time, and the bill's own fallback (certifications and delayed deadlines) shows its authors expected the transition to be hard. On balance the bill imposed accountability on an industry operating with limited oversight; the strongest objection is practical feasibility, not principle.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on February 23, 2010, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Armed Services [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and the Congress ended January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private military and security contractors kept their war-zone contracts and remained free from the quarterly congressional accounting, disclosure of casualties, and renewal conditions the bill would have imposed; agencies also avoided the cost of building a government workforce to replace contractors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private military contractors kept their contracts

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Outsourcing Security Act on February 23, 2010 to phase out private military contractors [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Carl Levin (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on February 23, 2010 and took no action—no hearing, no markup, no report—before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action, it was never scheduled for a vote.

against.name: Private military and security contractors
against.role: Industry including Blackwater/Xe, DynCorp, and ArmorGroup/Wackenhut, holding tens of thousands of armed personnel and billions in U.S. contracts in Iraq and Afghanistan
against.what_they_did: The bill's own findings document contractor misconduct, overbilling, and tax-avoidance; the industry had a direct financial stake in the status quo the bill would have ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party and no recorded votes, so the partisan shape of any opposition was never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Private military and security contractors (e.g., Blackwater/Xe, DynCorp, ArmorGroup)
industries.note: The bill would have phased out their core business—armed security, training, interrogation, and intelligence work in U.S. conflict zones—and subjected their contracts to congressional examination [S2][S3]. Their gain in the status quo is the public's cost: the findings document taxpayer overbilling, tax avoidance, and civilian deaths at contractor hands [S3].

industries.industry: Defense and diplomatic agencies' contractor workforce
industries.note: Roughly 218,000 DoD contract employees in Iraq and Afghanistan and thousands of State Department security contractors would have had to be replaced by government personnel, a major cost and reorganization [S3].
